content: Burmese tofu, originating from the Shan region, is distinct from Chinese tofu, which is traditionally made from soybeans. Shan tofu is prepared using yellow split peas, while the Burmese version utilizes besan flour (chickpea flour). The preparation involves mixing the flour with water, turmeric, and a small amount of salt, then heating the mixture while stirring continuously until it achieves a creamy consistency. This mixture is then poured into a tray and left to set. The resulting tofu is matte yellow in color, firm yet jelly-like in texture, and does not crumble when sliced. It can be consumed fresh in salads, deep-fried, or sliced and dried to create crackers for frying. In Myanmar, the term tofu (referred to as to hpu) is used to describe both Chinese tofu and its local variations. Stinky tofu, the fermented form of Chinese tofu, is called si to hpu, likely derived from the Chinese term chòu dòufu. The yellow tofu made from yellow split peas in Shan State is known as won ta hpo. Another variation, to hpu gyauk, refers to dried tofu sliced into thin rectangular shapes and sun-dried, resembling fish or prawn crackers and sold in bundles. The common Burmese tofu made from chickpea flour, known as to hpu, has a similar yellow color and taste but is slightly firmer than Shan tofu. A rice flour-based tofu called hsan ta hpo, primarily found in Shan regions, is white in color and has a similar consistency but a slightly different taste. It is as popular as the yellow tofu in salads. Fried tofu, or to hpu gyaw, involves cutting yellow tofu into rectangular shapes, scoring the middle, and deep-frying it. These fritters are crispy on the outside and soft on the inside, often served with a spicy sour dip or incorporated into salads. A variation called hnapyan gyaw involves frying the tofu twice after cutting it into triangular shapes, a traditional method in Shan State. Another version, to hpu gyauk kyaw, refers to deep-fried tofu crackers, typically served with rice balls kneaded with fish or potato (htamin gyin) or with glutinous rice (kau hnyin baung) as a breakfast option. Fried tofu pairs well with dishes like mohinga (rice vermicelli in fish soup) or Shan rice noodles (hsan hkauk swè). Green tea is the traditional beverage accompanying these meals in Burma. Tofu salad, or to hpu thouk, is a popular snack or standalone meal. Fresh tofu, cut into small rectangular slices, serves as the main ingredient, dressed with peanut oil, dark soy sauce, rice vinegar, toasted crushed dried chili, crushed garlic, crushed roasted peanuts, crisp-fried onions, and coriander. A variation, to hpu gyaw thouk, uses tofu fritters cut up and served as a salad. Another form, to hpu nway (warm tofu) or to hpu byaw (soft tofu), is served hot before it sets, often as a salad with similar garnishes. This creamy tofu can be combined with tofu fritters or rice noodles in the same dish. Yellow tofu can also be curried, a dish known as to hpu gyet. Sliced yellow tofu is cooked with fresh tomatoes, onions, and garlic in peanut oil and fish sauce, then garnished with coriander and green chili. This dish is a popular pescatarian option served with rice and is also favored by those who cannot afford meat or poultry. Besan flour, also called gram flour, is made from chana dal (Bengal gram), a type of small, dark-colored chickpea commonly used in Indian cuisine. Rice tofu salad (hsan ta hpo thouk) from Shan State is as popular as the yellow Burmese tofu salad. Shan rice noodles (Shan hkauk swè) served with tofu fritters (to hpu gyaw) and pickled mustard greens (monnyin gyin) are a well-loved combination. A salad combining warm Burmese tofu (to hpu nway) and tofu fritters (to hpu gyaw) offers a satisfying mix of creamy and crispy textures.
